CHIEF COMPLAINT
Positive hepatitis C lab work found on routine screening.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient is a male presenting with incidental finding of positive hepatitis C antibody on routine physical examination screening. Patient reports feeling well and was surprised by the positive result. He denies prior diagnosis of hepatitis C. Patient has a significant past history of intravenous drug use but reports being clean for over 15 years. He continues to drink alcohol, consuming a beer daily, though less than in the past. He smokes 1-2 cigarettes per day and has attempted to reduce consumption. Patient is concerned about transmission to his wife and children.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Patient denies jaundice, abdominal pain, or other hepatic symptoms. No systemic complaints reported.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
No significant medical conditions reported. Recent physical examination otherwise unremarkable.

MEDICATIONS
Patient reports taking no medications.

ALLERGIES
Not documented.

FAMILY HISTORY
Hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and depression.

SOCIAL HISTORY
Former intravenous drug user, clean for 15+ years. Current alcohol use: beer daily. Current tobacco use: 1-2 cigarettes per day. Married with children.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: Within normal limits. General: No distress, no jaundice. Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm with grade 2/6 systolic ejection murmur. Pulmonary: Clear to auscultation bilaterally, no wheezes, rales, or rhonchi. Abdomen: Soft, bowel sounds present, no hepatosplenomegaly. Neurological: No gait disturbance or edema.

RESULTS
HCV antibody: Positive. Liver panel: AST elevated at 39 U/L; ALT, albumin, and total bilirubin within normal limits.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Hepatitis C infection. Patient counseled that hepatitis C is a chronic viral infection affecting the liver, likely present for several years with minimal symptoms to date. Plan: (1) Confirm diagnosis with HCV RNA and HCV genotype testing; (2) Assess liver fibrosis severity with ultrasound elastography; (3) Screen wife and children with HCV antibody testing and coordinate care with family physician; (4) Follow-up appointment in 3 weeks to review results and determine treatment approach.
